options: Declares that a block starts a brand-new transaction fully independent of whatever transaction called it
Disables all transaction logging for a session
Forces a block to always run inside the caller's exact transaction
Automatically rolls back every INSERT inside the block
questions.explain: An autonomous transaction can COMMIT or ROLLBACK on its own, with no effect on, or from, the calling transaction.

questions.q: What real-world problem do autonomous transactions solve?
options: Letting a log/audit record persist even if the main transaction that triggered it later rolls back
Making SELECT statements run faster
Allowing a procedure to skip the EXCEPTION section entirely
Preventing any transaction from ever being rolled back
questions.explain: The classic use case is logging that an attempt was made, regardless of whether the attempt's main transaction ultimately succeeded or failed.

questions.q: What happens if an autonomous block exits without an explicit COMMIT or ROLLBACK?
options: Oracle raises ORA-06519 and rolls back the autonomous work itself
Oracle automatically commits the work silently
The calling transaction is automatically rolled back instead
Nothing — autonomous transactions don't require either statement
questions.explain: Oracle strictly enforces this rule; forgetting COMMIT or ROLLBACK in an autonomous block raises an error.

questions.q: Why can't T-SQL's nested BEGIN TRANSACTION calls replicate autonomous transaction behavior?
options: SQL Server tracks a single nesting count, and an outer ROLLBACK undoes everything, including logically 'inner' work
T-SQL nested transactions are already fully independent, just with different syntax
T-SQL doesn't support BEGIN TRANSACTION at all
T-SQL nested transactions always commit immediately regardless of the outer transaction
questions.explain: T-SQL has no mechanism for a block to commit its own work irrevocably while a surrounding transaction is still pending — exactly the gap autonomous transactions fill.

questions.q: In the transfer_funds example, why does the login_audit row survive even when the fund transfer itself fails and rolls back?
options: Because log_login_attempt runs as an autonomous transaction and already committed before the failure occurred
Because login_audit is a temp table that is never affected by ROLLBACK
Because RAISE_APPLICATION_ERROR only rolls back SELECT statements, not INSERTs
Because autonomous transactions are rolled back only after a 24-hour delay
questions.explain: The autonomous procedure's COMMIT already happened independently, before the outer transaction's later failure and rollback.
